title: Pronoun Reference: What Does 'It' Refer To?
summary: How to answer reading questions about what it, this, they or which refers to, the types of pronoun, and how to use pronouns clearly and correctly in your own writing, with practice and answers.

blocks.text: A **pronoun** replaces a noun so that the writer does not have to repeat it. The noun it replaces is called its **antecedent** (the word that goes before). *The museum reopened last week. **It** had been closed for two years.* → *It* refers to *the museum*.
Reading questions often ask you **what a pronoun refers to**. In your own writing, every pronoun must point clearly to one noun, or the reader gets confused.

blocks.title: Key words
items: **Pronoun**: a word that replaces a noun (*it, they, she, this, which*).
**Antecedent**: the noun or idea a pronoun refers back to.
**Ambiguous**: having more than one possible meaning, so the reader cannot tell which noun is meant.

rows: Subject
I, you, he, she, it, we, they
**They** arrived early.
Object
me, you, him, her, it, us, them
The coach praised **them**.
Possessive adjective
my, your, his, her, its, our, their
**Their** bus was late.
Possessive pronoun
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
The red bag is **hers**.
Reflexive
myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves
She taught **herself** to code.
Demonstrative
this, that, these, those
**This** changed everything.
Relative
who, which, that, whose, where
The girl **who** won the race is my cousin.

blocks.text: 3. How to answer 'What does it / this / they refer to?'

items: **Look backwards** from the pronoun to the nearest noun that matches it in number (singular *it* → a singular noun, plural *they* → a plural noun).
**Check meaning**: put your answer in place of the pronoun. Does the sentence still make sense?
**This / that / these / such** can refer to a **whole idea or sentence**, not just one word. Then your answer should sum up the idea.
**Write the full noun phrase**, not just one word (*the old lighthouse on the cliff*, not *lighthouse*).

blocks.text: **Worked example.** *Every spring, storks arrive in the Nile Delta after a journey of thousands of kilometres. **They** build huge nests on rooftops and poles. Local farmers welcome **this**, because the birds eat insects that damage **their** crops.*

rows: They
the storks
Plural. The storks are the ones who arrive and build nests
this
the storks building nests on rooftops and poles (the whole idea)
*This* sums up the whole previous sentence
their
the local farmers
The crops belong to the farmers, not the birds

blocks.title: Traps in reference questions
items: The nearest noun is **not always** the answer: check the meaning. *The dog chased the cat until **it** was tired* could mean either animal, so the context decides.
Do not answer with another pronoun (*it refers to it*). Always give the noun.
Relative pronouns can be asked too: in *the village **which** I visited*, *which* refers to *the village*.

blocks.text: **Avoid unclear (ambiguous) pronouns.** *Omar told Karim that he had won.* (who won?) → *Omar told Karim, "You've won!"* or *Omar told Karim that Karim had won.*

**Make pronouns agree** with their antecedent in number: *The blankets were dirty, so we washed **them**.* For a singular word like *every student*, the safest choice in formal writing is *his or her*, or make the subject plural: *All students should bring their notebooks.*
**Use the right case**: subject pronouns before the verb, object pronouns after verbs and prepositions.

rows: Me and Ali went to the park.
Ali and I went to the park.
Subject position needs *I*. Put the other person first.
The teacher gave the books to Ali and I.
The teacher gave the books to Ali and me.
After a preposition (*to*), use the object form *me*.
Between you and I, it was a mistake.
Between you and me, it was a mistake.
*between* is a preposition: object form.
Please contact myself if you have questions.
Please contact me if you have questions.
Use a reflexive only when the subject and object are the same person.
The company changed it's logo.
The company changed its logo.
*its* = belonging to it. *it's* = it is.
Everyone must bring their own pen. (very formal tasks)
All students must bring their own pens.
Making the subject plural avoids the problem in formal writing.
The film was long and boring, which annoyed me. It was a waste of money.
Clear: *It* = the film.
Fine, but check that *which* and *it* each point to one clear idea.

blocks.text: **Pronouns for cohesion.** Good writers use pronouns and *this / these + noun* to link sentences smoothly without repeating words: *The council has closed the sports centre. **This decision** has angered many families.* Adding a noun after *this* (*this decision, this problem, these changes*) makes the link clearer and more formal.

**In reading**, a typical question is: *What does the word 'it' (or 'this', 'they', 'which') in line X refer to?* Give the **full noun phrase** or a **short summary of the idea**. One mark usually needs the exact thing, not a vague guess.
**Exam-style example.** *Scientists have found that teenagers who sleep less than eight hours find it harder to concentrate. This may explain why many students struggle in morning lessons.*
**Question:** What does *This* refer to? **Answer:** The finding that teenagers who sleep less than eight hours find it harder to concentrate.
**In your writing**, use pronouns to avoid repetition, keep every reference clear, and use *this / these + noun* to link paragraphs.

blocks.title: سؤال الضمير بيرجع على إيه
items: ارجع لورا من الضمير ودوّر على الاسم اللي يناسبه: it مفرد، they جمع.
جرّب تحط الإجابة مكان الضمير، لو الجملة مفهومة يبقى صح.
this ممكن ترجع على فكرة الجملة كلها، ساعتها اكتب الفكرة باختصار.
اكتب الاسم كامل (the old mill) مش كلمة واحدة.

items.q: Text: *The old mill stood beside the river for two hundred years. It ground flour for the whole valley. When it closed, many families lost their income.* What does *It* refer to, and what does *their* refer to?
items.a: *It* = the old mill. *their* = the many families (the income belonged to them).

items.q: Text: *The school replaced its plastic cups with metal bottles. This saved over ten thousand cups a year.* What does *This* refer to?
items.a: The whole action of replacing the plastic cups with metal bottles (the idea in the previous sentence), not just the bottles.

items.q: Text: *Desert foxes have enormous ears. These help them to hear insects moving under the sand.* What do *These* and *them* refer to?
items.a: *These* = the desert foxes' enormous ears. *them* = the desert foxes.

items.q: Text: *The village, which had no electricity until 1990, is now a popular stop for tourists.* What does *which* refer to?
Text: *Laila handed her grandmother the letter. She read it twice before she spoke.* What does *it* refer to?
Rewrite to remove the unclear pronoun: *When Tamer met his father at the airport, he was very tired.*
items.a: *Tamer was very tired when he met his father at the airport.* (or *When Tamer met his father at the airport, his father was very tired.*)

items.q: Correct: *My brother and me cleaned the car.*
items.a: *My brother and I cleaned the car.*

items.q: Correct: *The prize was shared between Hana and I.*
items.a: *The prize was shared between Hana and me.*

items.q: Correct: *Every player must wear their helmet.* (formal notice)
items.a: *All players must wear their helmets.* (or *Every player must wear his or her helmet.*)

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Look back for the matching noun, test it in place of the pronoun, and give the full noun phrase. In writing: one pronoun, one clear meaning.
